questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old boy presents with fair skin, blue eyes, and musty body odor. He has intellectual disability and seizures. Urine and blood amino acid analysis reveals markedly elevated phenylalanine. Which enzyme is deficient in this condition and what is the DIRECT biochemical consequence?

options.A: Tyrosinase deficiency → failure to convert tyrosine to DOPA
options.B: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency → accumulation of phenylalanine and its toxic metabolites (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate)
options.C: Homogentisate oxidase deficiency → accumulation of homogentisic acid
options.D: Fumarylacetoacetase deficiency → accumulation of fumarylacetoacetate

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which converts phenylalanine → tyrosine using tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as cofactor. Accumulated phenylalanine is transaminated to phenylpyruvate (phenylketone, giving the name), phenylacetate (musty/mousy odor), and phenyllactate. These metabolites are neurotoxic. Classic PKU features: fair skin/hair (tyrosine → melanin pathway impaired), intellectual disability, seizures, eczema. Incorrect options: (A) Tyrosinase deficiency causes oculocutaneous albinism — no intellectual disability or elevated phenylalanine. (C) Homogentisate oxidase deficiency causes alkaptonuria — dark urine, ochronosis, arthritis — no elevated phenylalanine. (D) Fumarylacetoacetase deficiency causes tyrosinemia type I (hepatorenal) — liver failure, cabbage-like odor, succinylacetone in urine. Exam pearl: BH4-responsive PKU: milder form, responds to sapropterin. Screening: Guthrie test (blood spot) at 48–72 hours. Treatment: Phe-restricted diet + tyrosine supplementation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man develops severe hemolytic anemia after taking primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. His RBCs show Heinz bodies on crystal violet staining. Enzyme assay reveals markedly reduced activity of the rate-limiting enzyme of the hexose monophosphate (pentose phosphate) pathway. Which enzyme is deficient?

options.A: Pyruvate kinase
options.B: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)
options.C: Phosphoglucose isomerase
options.D: Glutathione reductase

questions.explanation: Correct (B): G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymopathy worldwide. G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the hexose monophosphate shunt (HMP shunt / pentose phosphate pathway). It catalyzes: glucose-6-phosphate + NADP+ → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH. NADPH is essential for regenerating reduced glutathione (GSH), which protects RBCs from oxidative damage. Without G6PD → no NADPH → GSH depleted → oxidant stress → Heinz body formation (denatured Hb) → hemolysis. Triggers: primaquine, dapsone, fava beans, infections. Incorrect options: (A) Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic hemolytic anemia (not triggered by drugs) — Heinz bodies NOT typically seen; echinocytes seen instead. (C) Phosphoglucose isomerase deficiency is a rare cause of hemolytic anemia — not related to drug triggers or Heinz bodies. (D) Glutathione reductase deficiency impairs GSH regeneration but is not the primary or rate-limiting enzyme of the HMP shunt. Exam pearl: G6PD is X-linked recessive → affects males predominantly. Common in malaria-endemic regions (offers partial protection against P. falciparum). Heinz bodies = denatured Hb precipitates.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man presents with premature coronary artery disease. Lipid profile shows total cholesterol 340 mg/dL, LDL 280 mg/dL, triglycerides 120 mg/dL, and HDL 38 mg/dL. Genetic analysis reveals a mutation in the LDL receptor. Which of the following correctly describes the MECHANISM of LDL receptor-mediated endocytosis?

options.A: LDL binds to its receptor → clathrin-coated pit → endosome → VLDL secretion from liver
options.B: LDL binds ApoB-100 receptor on hepatocytes → receptor-mediated endocytosis via clathrin-coated pits → lysosomal degradation → free cholesterol suppresses HMG-CoA reductase and LDLR expression
options.C: LDL is phagocytosed by macrophages → foam cell formation → reduces hepatic cholesterol synthesis
options.D: LDL binds to scavenger receptor A on hepatocytes → activates cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase → bile acid synthesis

questions.explanation: Correct (B): LDL receptor (LDLR) on hepatocyte surfaces binds ApoB-100 (the structural apolipoprotein of LDL). The LDL-LDLR complex is internalized via clathrin-coated pits → endosomes → lysosomes. Cholesterol esters are hydrolyzed → free cholesterol. Free cholesterol then: (1) Suppresses HMG-CoA reductase (rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis), (2) Suppresses LDLR synthesis (downregulation), (3) Activates ACAT (stores as cholesterol ester). Familial hypercholesterolemia = LDLR mutation → LDL cannot be cleared → elevated LDL → atherosclerosis. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → upregulate LDLR (by SREBP pathway) → more LDL cleared. Incorrect options: (A) VLDL secretion by liver is a separate process from LDL receptor uptake. (C) Scavenger receptor-mediated LDL uptake by macrophages occurs in atherosclerotic plaques (foam cell formation) but is not receptor-mediated endocytosis via LDLR and does not directly reduce hepatic cholesterol. (D) Scavenger receptor A is on macrophages, not hepatocytes; cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase converts cholesterol to bile acids in the liver but is not activated by scavenger receptor. Exam pearl: Statins → HMG-CoA reductase inhibition → ↓ cholesterol → ↑ SREBP → ↑ LDLR expression → ↓ plasma LDL.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.image_title: Lineweaver-Burk double-reciprocal plot comparing inhibited and uninhibited enzyme kinetics
key_findings: Two lines: uninhibited enzyme and inhibited enzyme
Inhibited line has same X-intercept as uninhibited (same Km)
Inhibited line has higher Y-intercept (lower Vmax)
Lines do not intersect at same point on X-axis as in competitive inhibition
questions.question_text: A pharmaceutical company is developing an enzyme inhibitor. The Lineweaver-Burk plot shows that the new drug increases the Y-intercept (↑1/Vmax) but does NOT change the X-intercept (Km unchanged). Which type of inhibition does this represent?

options.A: Competitive inhibition
options.B: Uncompetitive inhibition
options.C: Non-competitive inhibition
options.D: Irreversible inhibition

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Non-competitive inhibition: The inhibitor binds to an allosteric site (different from the active site) on BOTH the free enzyme AND the enzyme-substrate complex. This does NOT affect substrate binding (Km unchanged) but reduces the catalytic efficiency (Vmax decreases). On the Lineweaver-Burk plot: Y-intercept increases (1/Vmax increases → Vmax decreases), X-intercept unchanged (Km unchanged), lines intersect on the X-axis. Incorrect options: (A) Competitive inhibition: Inhibitor competes with substrate at the active site. Km INCREASES (apparent), Vmax unchanged (can be overcome by excess substrate). LB plot: Y-intercept unchanged, X-intercept moves closer to origin. (B) Uncompetitive inhibition: Inhibitor binds ONLY the enzyme-substrate complex. BOTH Km AND Vmax decrease by the same factor. LB plot: parallel lines (same slope, both intercepts change). (D) Irreversible inhibition: Covalent modification of active site; Vmax decreases with no effect on Km for the remaining active enzyme molecules — similar kinetics to non-competitive but permanent. Exam pearl: Km interpretation: Km = substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity; lower Km = higher affinity. Vmax = maximum velocity when enzyme is saturated.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old alcoholic presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia. He later develops anterograde amnesia and confabulation. Which vitamin deficiency is responsible and what is its cofactor role?

options.A: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) — required for myelin synthesis via methionine synthase
options.B: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) — as TPP cofactor for α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes and transketolase
options.C: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) — as PLP cofactor for aminotransferases and decarboxylases
options.D: Niacin (B3) — as NAD+/NADH in oxidation-reduction reactions

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The clinical triad of confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia followed by Korsakoff's (amnesia + confabulation) = Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome due to thiamine (B1) deficiency, classically in alcoholics. Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is the active cofactor for: (1) Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) — pyruvate → acetyl-CoA. (2) Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (TCA cycle). (3) Branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase (BCKAD). (4) Transketolase (HMP shunt). Glucose infusion in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate acute Wernicke's (glucose → ↑pyruvate → overwhelms residual PDH). Always give thiamine BEFORE glucose. Incorrect options: (A) B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord (sensory ataxia + UMN signs), megaloblastic anemia, glossitis — not the acute ophthalmoplegic confusion picture. (C) B6 (PLP) deficiency: peripheral neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia, seborrheic dermatitis — not this acute syndrome. (D) Niacin (B3) deficiency causes Pellagra: Dermatitis, Diarrhea, Dementia (3Ds) — chronic, not acute ophthalmoplegia. Exam pearl: TPP-dependent enzymes mnemonic: PK Taxi (Pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, Transketolase, Alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase of BCAA).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A new antibiotic targets bacterial DNA replication by inhibiting the enzyme that relieves torsional stress ahead of the replication fork by transiently cutting and rejoining both strands of DNA. Which enzyme is this antibiotic inhibiting?

options.A: DNA polymerase III
options.B: DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II)
options.C: DNA primase
options.D: DNA helicase

questions.explanation: Correct (B): DNA gyrase (a type II topoisomerase) relieves positive supercoiling ahead of the replication fork by cutting BOTH strands of DNA, passing the DNA through the break, and religating. This prevents torsional stress buildup during replication. Quinolone antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV → accumulation of DNA breaks → bactericidal. Eukaryotic topoisomerase II is not significantly inhibited by fluoroquinolones (basis of selectivity). Incorrect options: (A) DNA pol III is the main replicative polymerase in bacteria (5'→3' synthesis with 3'→5' proofreading). Inhibited by: none of the classic antibiotics target pol III directly. (C) DNA primase synthesizes RNA primers at the origin and each Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand — not involved in supercoiling relief. (D) DNA helicase (DnaB in bacteria) unwinds the double helix at the replication fork — the torsional stress it CREATES is relieved by gyrase. Exam pearl: Quinolones: inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase + topoisomerase IV. Topoisomerase I: cuts one strand. Topoisomerase II (gyrase): cuts both strands.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 2-year-old girl presents with episodic hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and lactic acidosis during fasting. Enzyme studies show deficient activity of the enzyme that converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate. What is the diagnosis and the role of the deficient enzyme in gluconeogenesis?

options.A: Pyruvate kinase deficiency — first committed step of gluconeogenesis
options.B: Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency — pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → oxaloacetate (biotin-dependent), providing OAA for gluconeogenesis and TCA cycle
options.C: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) deficiency — converts malate to PEP
options.D: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency — commits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to gluconeogenesis

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Pyruvate carboxylase (PC) catalyzes: Pyruvate + CO2 + ATP → Oxaloacetate (using biotin as cofactor). This is the FIRST step of gluconeogenesis from pyruvate and lactate. Deficiency causes: (1) Hypoglycemia (cannot synthesize glucose), (2) Lactic acidosis (pyruvate accumulates, reduced to lactate), (3) Hyperammonemia (OAA needed for aspartate synthesis for urea cycle), (4) Mental retardation. PC is activated by acetyl-CoA (from fatty acid oxidation during fasting). Incorrect options: (A) Pyruvate kinase is a GLYCOLYTIC enzyme (PEP → pyruvate); its deficiency causes hemolytic anemia, not hypoglycemia. (C) PEPCK converts OAA → PEP + CO2 (the second step of gluconeogenesis, after PC). PEPCK deficiency also causes hypoglycemia but differently. (D) Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency causes hypoglycemia after fructose ingestion with lactic acidosis — a different enzyme. Exam pearl: Biotin-dependent carboxylases: PC, Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, Propionyl-CoA carboxylase, Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase. Avidin in raw egg whites blocks biotin → biotin deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 16-year-old type 1 diabetic presents with polyuria, vomiting, and fruity breath. ABG shows pH 7.10, pCO2 20 mmHg, HCO3 6 mEq/L. Urine shows 4+ ketones. Which enzyme is the RATE-LIMITING step for ketone body synthesis in the liver?

options.A: Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase
options.B: HMG-CoA synthase (mitochondrial)
options.C: HMG-CoA lyase
options.D: Beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Ketogenesis occurs in hepatic mitochondria. The pathway: 2 Acetyl-CoA → Acetoacetyl-CoA (thiolase) → HMG-CoA (HMG-CoA synthase, mitochondrial) → Acetoacetate (HMG-CoA lyase) + Acetyl-CoA → beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). The rate-limiting step is MITOCHONDRIAL HMG-CoA synthase (distinct from cytosolic HMG-CoA synthase involved in cholesterol synthesis). In DKA: insulin deficiency → unopposed glucagon → ↑ lipolysis → ↑ fatty acid oxidation → ↑ acetyl-CoA → ↑ ketogenesis. Fruity breath = acetone (spontaneous decarboxylation of acetoacetate). Incorrect options: (A) Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase is the FIRST step — not rate-limiting; also involved in beta-oxidation. (C) HMG-CoA lyase cleaves HMG-CoA to release acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA — important but not rate-limiting. (D) Beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase converts acetoacetate ↔ BHB — not rate-limiting. Exam pearl: Liver makes ketone bodies but CANNOT use them (lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase). Brain, heart, muscle use ketones. DKA: pH <7.3, HCO3 <15, high AG, hyperglycemia, ketonemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: Rifampicin is used to treat tuberculosis. It acts by binding to the beta subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase, blocking the initiation of transcription. Eukaryotic cells are spared because they have three different RNA polymerases. Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes ribosomal RNA (rRNA)?

options.A: RNA polymerase I
options.B: RNA polymerase II
options.C: RNA polymerase III
options.D: Primase (RNA polymerase delta)

questions.explanation: Correct (A): In eukaryotes, there are three nuclear RNA polymerases: (1) RNA Pol I: transcribes large ribosomal RNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S rRNA) — found in the nucleolus. (2) RNA Pol II: transcribes mRNA (protein-coding genes), snRNA, miRNA — alpha-amanitin (Amanita phalloides mushroom toxin) at low concentrations inhibits Pol II. (3) RNA Pol III: transcribes small RNAs — tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNA (U6) — inhibited by alpha-amanitin at very high concentrations. Incorrect options: (B) RNA Pol II transcribes mRNA → protein synthesis templates. It is the most complex (12 subunits) and is the target of alpha-amanitin. (C) RNA Pol III transcribes tRNA and 5S rRNA. (D) Primase is a special RNA polymerase that makes short RNA primers for DNA replication — not involved in transcription of structural RNAs. Exam pearl: Alpha-amanitin: Pol II (low conc) > Pol III (high conc). Pol I not inhibited. Actinomycin D: intercalates DNA, inhibits ALL RNA polymerases (used in cancer). Rifampicin: ONLY bacterial RNA polymerase (prokaryotic beta subunit).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 6-month-old exclusively breastfed infant living in a northern city presents with bowing of the legs, craniotabes, and a rachitic rosary. X-ray shows cupping and fraying of the metaphyses. Serum calcium is low-normal, phosphate is low, alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated, and PTH is elevated. Which vitamin deficiency is present and what is its active form?

options.A: Vitamin A deficiency — active form: all-trans-retinoic acid
options.B: Vitamin D deficiency — active form: 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol)
options.C: Vitamin K deficiency — active form: menaquinone-4
options.D: Vitamin E deficiency — active form: alpha-tocopherol

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The clinical picture is classic nutritional rickets due to Vitamin D deficiency. Active form = 1,25-(OH)2-D3 (calcitriol), produced by: Skin (UV-B) → cholecalciferol (D3) → Liver (25-hydroxylation, CYP27A1) → 25-(OH)-D3 (storage form) → Kidney (1-alpha-hydroxylation, CYP27B1, stimulated by PTH, low phosphate) → 1,25-(OH)2-D3 (active). Actions: ↑ intestinal Ca/P absorption, ↑ renal Ca reabsorption, ↑ bone mineralization. Deficiency → ↓Ca/P → secondary hyperparathyroidism (↑PTH) → bone demineralization (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults). Incorrect options: (A) Vitamin A deficiency: night blindness, keratomalacia, Bitot's spots — not bowed legs or rachitic changes. (C) Vitamin K deficiency: bleeding diathesis (prolonged PT), neonatal hemorrhagic disease — not bone changes. (D) Vitamin E deficiency: hemolytic anemia in premature infants, spinocerebellar degeneration — not rickets. Exam pearl: 25-(OH)-D3 is the SERUM MEASUREMENT for vitamin D status. 1,25-(OH)2-D3 is the ACTIVE form. Activated by PTH and hypophosphatemia. Inactivated by 24-hydroxylase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 3-year-old boy presents with massive hepatomegaly, severe hypoglycemia despite glucagon injection (no glucose response), and elevated blood lactate. Liver biopsy shows excess glycogen and fat. Enzyme analysis reveals absent glucose-6-phosphatase. Which glycogen storage disease is this and why does glucagon fail?

options.A: Pompe disease (Type II) — lysosomal alpha-glucosidase deficiency
options.B: Von Gierke disease (Type I) — glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency → G6P cannot be dephosphorylated to release free glucose
options.C: McArdle disease (Type V) — muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency
options.D: Cori disease (Type III) — debranching enzyme deficiency

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Von Gierke disease (GSD Type Ia) is caused by deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase (expressed only in liver, kidney, intestine). This enzyme catalyzes the FINAL step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis: glucose-6-phosphate → glucose + Pi. Without it, G6P accumulates → shunted into: glycolysis (→ lactate → lactic acidosis), HMP shunt (→ uric acid → hyperuricemia), lipid synthesis (→ hyperlipidemia). Glucagon normally stimulates glycogenolysis, but without G6P phosphatase, the glucose cannot be released from G6P → no rise in blood glucose → 'glucagon unresponsive.' Incorrect options: (A) Pompe disease: lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency — primarily affects heart and muscle (cardiomegaly, myopathy), not liver hypoglycemia. (C) McArdle disease: muscle-only glycogen phosphorylase deficiency — muscle cramps on exercise, myoglobinuria, NO liver involvement. (D) Cori disease: limit dextrin accumulates; milder than Von Gierke; gluconeogenesis is preserved (can still release some glucose). Exam pearl: Von Gierke = severe FASTING hypoglycemia + massive hepatomegaly + lactic acidosis + hyperlipidemia + hyperuricemia. Glucagon test: no response.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 2-day-old neonate presents with lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, and respiratory alkalosis. Plasma ammonia is 900 μmol/L (normal <50). Plasma amino acids show elevated glutamine and alanine, and plasma citrulline is ABSENT. Orotic acid in urine is elevated. Which enzyme of the urea cycle is most likely deficient?

options.A: Arginosuccinate synthetase → elevated citrulline
options.B: Ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) → X-linked, elevated orotic acid, absent citrulline
options.C: Carbamyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) → low orotic acid
options.D: Arginase → elevated arginine

questions.explanation: Correct (B): OTC deficiency (ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency) is the most common urea cycle disorder and the only X-linked one. OTC catalyzes: ornithine + carbamoyl phosphate → citrulline (in mitochondria). Deficiency → carbamoyl phosphate cannot enter cycle → accumulates → leaks into cytosol → feeds pyrimidine synthesis → ELEVATED OROTIC ACID in urine (characteristic). Citrulline is ABSENT (or very low). Ammonia accumulates → encephalopathy. Respiratory alkalosis = early (ammonia directly stimulates hyperventilation). Incorrect options: (A) Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (Type II citrullinemia) = ELEVATED citrulline in blood, NOT absent. (C) CPS I deficiency: low orotic acid (carbamoyl phosphate does not accumulate in cytosol) AND absent citrulline — differentiated by URINE OROTIC ACID (CPS I = low, OTC = high). (D) Arginase deficiency: elevated ARGININE, spastic diplegia, mild hyperammonemia in older children — not the acute neonatal presentation. Exam pearl: Elevated urine orotic acid + hyperammonemia = OTC deficiency (RULE OUT CPS I which has LOW orotic acid). OTC = X-linked; all other urea cycle disorders = autosomal recessive.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A researcher is studying the regulation of fatty acid synthesis. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) is the rate-limiting enzyme. Which of the following correctly describes the ALLOSTERIC regulation of ACC?

options.A: Activated by palmitoyl-CoA (end-product inhibition); inhibited by citrate
options.B: Activated by citrate (from TCA cycle when energy is high); inhibited by palmitoyl-CoA (end-product inhibition)
options.C: Activated by cAMP-dependent phosphorylation; inhibited by insulin
options.D: Activated by glucagon; inhibited by AMP kinase

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) converts acetyl-CoA + CO2 + ATP → malonyl-CoA (biotin-dependent, rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis). Regulation: (1) ALLOSTERIC ACTIVATION: Citrate — signals that energy (acetyl-CoA) is abundant in the TCA cycle; citrate exports acetyl-CoA from mitochondria as citrate → ACC is activated in the cytosol. (2) ALLOSTERIC INHIBITION: Palmitoyl-CoA (long-chain fatty acyl-CoA) — end-product feedback inhibition. (3) HORMONAL: Insulin → activates (dephosphorylation by phosphatase). Glucagon/epinephrine → inhibits (AMPK phosphorylates and inactivates ACC). (4) AMP kinase (AMPK) = cellular energy sensor → phosphorylates ACC → inhibits fatty acid synthesis when energy is low. Incorrect options: (A) Palmitoyl-CoA inhibits (correct) but citrate ACTIVATES (not inhibits). (C) cAMP-dependent phosphorylation INACTIVATES ACC (via PKA → AMPK pathway); insulin dephosphorylates = activates. (D) Glucagon INHIBITS ACC; AMPK also inhibits ACC. Exam pearl: Fed state: insulin → ↑ACC → ↑fatty acid synthesis. Fasted state: glucagon/epinephrine → ↑AMPK → ↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑carnitine acyltransferase I → ↑beta-oxidation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old boy presents with self-mutilation behavior (biting of fingers and lips), choreoathetosis, intellectual disability, and gout. His uric acid levels are markedly elevated. Urine shows orange crystals. Which enzyme is deficient?

options.A: Adenosine deaminase (ADA)
options.B: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP)
options.C: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT)
options.D: Xanthine oxidase

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: X-linked recessive deficiency of HGPRT. This enzyme is required for the SALVAGE pathway of purines: hypoxanthine + PRPP → IMP; guanine + PRPP → GMP. Without HGPRT, purines cannot be salvaged → excess de novo purine synthesis → hypoxanthine → xanthine → URIC ACID (by xanthine oxidase). Features: hyperuricemia + gout (uric acid crystals in urine), neurological (choreoathetosis, spasticity, intellectual disability), and pathognomonic SELF-MUTILATION (lip/finger biting). Incorrect options: (A) ADA deficiency: accumulation of deoxyadenosine → toxic to lymphocytes → Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) — immune deficiency, NOT gout or self-mutilation. (B) PNP deficiency: T-cell immunodeficiency (adenosine accumulates in T cells) — immune deficiency. (D) Xanthine oxidase deficiency: xanthinuria — decreased uric acid, xanthine crystals in urine — NOT hyperuricemia. Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase to TREAT gout/Lesch-Nyhan. Exam pearl: Lesch-Nyhan: hyperuricemia + SELF-MUTILATION + neurological. X-linked. Treatment: allopurinol for hyperuricemia (does NOT improve neurological symptoms).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A pharmaceutical researcher is studying proteasomal degradation. Proteins destined for proteasomal destruction are tagged by a small protein before entering the 26S proteasome. Which of the following best describes this tagging process?

options.A: Glycosylation with mannose-6-phosphate signals lysosomal targeting
options.B: Ubiquitin is covalently attached via an isopeptide bond to lysine residues of the target protein, mediated by E1 (activating), E2 (conjugating), E3 (ligase) enzymes
options.C: SUMOylation by small ubiquitin-like modifier targets protein for proteasomal degradation
options.D: PEST sequence (Pro-Glu-Ser-Thr) directly activates caspase-mediated cleavage

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is the major pathway for intracellular protein degradation. Process: E1 (ubiquitin-activating enzyme) activates ubiquitin using ATP → transfers to E2 (conjugating enzyme) → E3 (ubiquitin ligase) recognizes specific protein substrates and catalyzes transfer of ubiquitin to the lysine ε-amino group (isopeptide bond). A polyubiquitin chain (≥4 ubiquitin molecules) signals entry into the 26S proteasome (19S regulatory cap + 20S catalytic core). The substrate is unfolded and degraded to short peptides. Incorrect options: (A) Mannose-6-phosphate tagging targets proteins to LYSOSOMES (not proteasomes) — used for lysosomal enzymes (I-cell disease = defect in this pathway). (C) SUMOylation modifies protein interactions, localization, and transcription — it generally does NOT directly target proteins for proteasomal degradation (unlike ubiquitin). (D) PEST sequences are internal degradation signals that may promote ubiquitination but do not directly activate caspases. Caspases are cysteine proteases activated in apoptosis. Exam pearl: E3 ubiquitin ligases determine substrate specificity. MDM2 = E3 for p53 (ubiquitinates p53 → degradation). In cancer, MDM2 amplification → ↓p53. Proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib) → treat multiple myeloma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old type 2 diabetic on metformin is admitted with acute kidney injury. He develops severe lactic acidosis (lactate 12 mmol/L, pH 7.1). Metformin's primary mechanism involves inhibition of which complex in the mitochondrial electron transport chain that leads to lactate accumulation?

options.A: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase)
options.B: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase / NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase)
options.C: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase)
options.D: Complex V (ATP synthase)

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Metformin inhibits Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. This reduces ATP production from OXPHOS → AMP:ATP ratio rises → AMPK activation (→ beneficial metabolic effects). Inhibition of Complex I also reduces NADH oxidation → increased NADH:NAD+ ratio → lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) shifts equilibrium toward LACTATE formation (pyruvate + NADH + H+ → lactate + NAD+). In renal failure, metformin accumulates (renally excreted) → severe Complex I inhibition → life-threatening lactic acidosis. Incorrect options: (A) Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase / SDH): part of TCA cycle and ETC; inhibited by malonate; mutations cause paraganglioma/pheochromocytoma — not the metformin target. (C) Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase): inhibited by cyanide, CO, azide — not metformin. (D) Complex V (ATP synthase): inhibited by oligomycin — not metformin. Exam pearl: Metformin contraindicated in renal failure (eGFR <30), liver failure, congestive heart failure, contrast use — risk of lactic acidosis. Does NOT cause hypoglycemia alone (no insulin secretion). First-line T2DM drug.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.image_title: Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve showing normal and shifted curves
key_findings: S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve representing cooperative oxygen binding
Right shift of curve in acidosis, hyperthermia, high 2,3-DPG, high CO2
Left shift in alkalosis, hypothermia, low 2,3-DPG, high CO (CO poisoning), fetal Hb
Bohr effect illustrated by pH-dependent shift
questions.question_text: A mountaineer at high altitude (5,000 m) shows adaptation over weeks including increased red cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG). Referring to the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve shown, what is the DIRECT effect of increased 2,3-BPG on hemoglobin function?

options.A: Shifts curve LEFT → increased oxygen affinity → better oxygen loading in lungs
options.B: Shifts curve RIGHT → decreased oxygen affinity → facilitates oxygen unloading to tissues
options.C: Increases Vmax of hemoglobin without changing P50
options.D: Causes conversion of oxyhemoglobin to methemoglobin

questions.explanation: Correct (B): 2,3-BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate) is synthesized in RBCs via the Rapoport-Luebering shunt (from 1,3-BPG). It binds to the central cavity of DEOXYHEMOGLOBIN (T-state), stabilizing it and reducing oxygen affinity. Effect: RIGHT SHIFT of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve → lower oxygen affinity → increased P50 → oxygen MORE READILY RELEASED to tissues. At high altitude, hypoxia → ↑2,3-BPG production → RIGHT shift → more O2 delivered to tissues despite lower pO2. Incorrect options: (A) Left shift = INCREASED O2 affinity (less unloading to tissues) — seen in alkalosis, hypothermia, fetal HbF (HbF has lower affinity for 2,3-BPG → left shift → fetal blood extracts O2 from maternal blood). (C) Hemoglobin is NOT an enzyme — Vmax does not apply. (D) Methemoglobin formation (Fe2+ → Fe3+) is caused by oxidizing agents (nitrites, dapsone, benzocaine) — not by 2,3-BPG. Exam pearl: RIGHT shift causes: ↑ temperature, ↓ pH (acidosis), ↑ CO2, ↑ 2,3-BPG = 'Bohr effect' facilitates O2 release. Fetal HbF = left shift (binds 2,3-BPG poorly) = higher O2 affinity than adult HbA (extracts O2 from maternal blood).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 5-year-old child presents with hyperextensible joints, fragile skin that bruises easily, and poor wound healing. Biopsy shows abnormal collagen fibers. Biochemical studies show adequate vitamin C levels. The defect is in an enzyme that hydroxylates lysine and proline residues in the ER. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

options.A: Lysyl oxidase (extracellular cross-linking enzyme)
options.B: Prolyl hydroxylase or lysyl hydroxylase (ER, vitamin C-dependent)
options.C: Signal peptidase (removes signal peptide in ER)
options.D: Procollagen N-proteinase

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Collagen synthesis (intracellular steps): Ribosomes → preprocollagen → signal peptide cleavage → procollagen in RER → Hydroxylation of Pro and Lys (PROLYL HYDROXYLASE and LYSYL HYDROXYLASE — require vitamin C, O2, Fe2+, alpha-ketoglutarate) → Glycosylation of hydroxylysine → Triple helix formation → Procollagen secreted. In this case, vitamin C levels are adequate, so the defect is in the ENZYME ITSELF (lysyl hydroxylase or prolyl hydroxylase), causing Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (kyphoscoliosis type, EDS type VI — lysyl hydroxylase deficiency). The hydroxyl groups are needed for hydrogen bonding stabilizing the triple helix and for cross-link formation. Incorrect options: (A) Lysyl oxidase is an EXTRACELLULAR enzyme that forms aldol cross-links between lysine/hydroxylysine residues — its deficiency causes cutis laxa, Menkes disease. Not the described hydroxylation step in ER. (C) Signal peptidase removes the N-terminal signal peptide — defects here are lethal. (D) Procollagen N-proteinase cleaves the N-propeptide in the EXTRACELLULAR space — deficiency causes dermatosparaxis (EDS type VII). Exam pearl: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) → defective hydroxylation of Pro/Lys → unstable triple helix → defective collagen → bleeding, poor wound healing, corkscrew hairs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 3-week-old neonate presents with jaundice, vomiting, hepatomegaly, and E. coli sepsis after beginning breast milk feeds. Reducing substances are found in urine (positive Benedict's test, negative glucose oxidase strip). Which diagnosis fits best?

options.A: Hereditary fructose intolerance — aldolase B deficiency
options.B: Classic galactosemia — galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency
options.C: Galactokinase deficiency — milder form causing cataracts only
options.D: Lactase deficiency — osmotic diarrhea, not jaundice

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Classic galactosemia is caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT). Galactose (from lactose in breast milk) → galactose-1-phosphate (galactokinase) → BLOCKED. Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate is toxic to liver, brain, and kidneys. Features: (1) Jaundice/liver disease, (2) Cataract (galactitol accumulation via aldose reductase), (3) E. coli sepsis (galactosemia increases susceptibility), (4) Intellectual disability, (5) Reducing substances in urine (galactose is a reducing sugar — positive Benedict's but NEGATIVE glucose oxidase, which is specific for glucose). Incorrect options: (A) Hereditary fructose intolerance (aldolase B deficiency): presents only after FRUCTOSE exposure (fruit juices, sucrose) — not in a breast-milk-fed neonate. (C) Galactokinase deficiency: milder, causes cataracts only (galactitol accumulates) without liver disease or sepsis. (D) Lactase deficiency: osmotic diarrhea, bloating — not jaundice or E. coli sepsis. Exam pearl: Galactosemia: remove lactose from diet immediately (soy formula). Neonatal E. coli sepsis in a jaundiced baby → think galactosemia. Gal-1-P accumulation = toxin. Galactokinase deficiency = cataracts only (milder).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A drug company develops a monoclonal antibody targeting HER2 (ErbB2), a receptor tyrosine kinase overexpressed in some breast cancers. Which intracellular signaling cascade is primarily activated when HER2 is stimulated, and which drug already on the market uses this mechanism?

options.A: G-protein → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → PKA (trastuzumab)
options.B: HER2 homodimerization/heterodimerization → intrinsic tyrosine kinase activation → Ras/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways → cell proliferation (trastuzumab blocks HER2 extracellularly)
options.C: JAK-STAT pathway → nuclear translocation of STAT → gene expression (cetuximab)
options.D: TGF-beta → SMAD pathway → anti-proliferative signal

questions.explanation: Correct (B): HER2 (ErbB2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) of the ErbB family. When overexpressed, it forms homodimers or heterodimers (with HER1/EGFR, HER3, HER4) → constitutive activation of intrinsic tyrosine kinase → phosphorylation cascade activating: (1) Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK (MAPK pathway) → cell proliferation, (2) PI3K → PIP3 → PDK1 → Akt (PI3K/Akt pathway) → cell survival/anti-apoptosis. Trastuzumab (Herceptin) is a monoclonal antibody that binds domain IV of HER2's extracellular region → blocks signaling + induces ADCC (antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity). Incorrect options: (A) G-protein/cAMP/PKA is the pathway used by GPCRs (e.g., beta-adrenergic receptors, glucagon receptor) — not RTKs. (C) JAK-STAT is used by cytokine receptors (interferons, interleukins, growth hormone). Cetuximab targets EGFR (HER1), not HER2. (D) TGF-beta/SMAD is a TUMOR SUPPRESSOR pathway — anti-proliferative. Exam pearl: RTK signaling: Ligand → dimerization → trans-autophosphorylation → adaptor proteins (Grb2/SOS) → Ras activation → MAPK or PI3K/Akt. Pertuzumab blocks HER2 dimerization (different from trastuzumab).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman on isoniazid therapy for tuberculosis develops peripheral neuropathy with burning sensations in the hands and feet. Which vitamin deficiency explains this complication, and what is the mechanism of isoniazid-induced deficiency?

options.A: Vitamin B12 — isoniazid blocks intrinsic factor
options.B: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) — isoniazid is a hydrazide that binds and inactivates pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) and increases urinary excretion of pyridoxine
options.C: Niacin — isoniazid inhibits nicotinamide synthesis from tryptophan
options.D: Folate — isoniazid inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Isoniazid (INH) is a hydrazide compound. It reacts with pyridoxal (vitamin B6 aldehyde form) to form inactive hydrazones, and also increases renal excretion of pyridoxine. PLP (pyridoxal phosphate) is the active coenzyme form of B6, essential for: (1) Transamination (all aminotransferases), (2) Decarboxylation (DOPA, 5-HTP → serotonin), (3) Heme synthesis (ALA synthase), (4) Glycogenolysis (glycogen phosphorylase), (5) Sphingolipid synthesis. Functional PLP deficiency → peripheral neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia, seborrheic dermatitis. Prevention: give pyridoxine (25–50 mg/day) with INH. Incorrect options: (A) B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration, megaloblastic anemia — not caused by INH. B12 uptake requires intrinsic factor but INH doesn't block this. (C) INH actually interferes with niacin synthesis secondarily (isoniazid and nicotinic acid have structural similarity), but the PRIMARY deficiency is B6. (D) Methotrexate, trimethoprim, pyrimethamine, and proguanil inhibit DHFR — NOT isoniazid. Exam pearl: B6 cofactor = PLP = pyridoxal phosphate. Deficiency causes sideroblastic anemia (ALA synthase requires PLP) + neuropathy + glossitis. INH → B6 deficiency → give pyridoxine prophylactically.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 6-month-old Ashkenazi Jewish infant develops psychomotor regression, hyperacusis, exaggerated startle response, cherry-red spot on fundoscopy, and macrocephaly. Enzyme assay reveals absent hexosaminidase A activity. Which lipid accumulates in neurons?

options.A: Glucocerebroside (glucosylceramide)
options.B: GM2 ganglioside
options.C: Galactocerebroside
options.D: Sphingomyelin

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Tay-Sachs disease: autosomal recessive deficiency of hexosaminidase A (the alpha subunit of Hex A). Hex A normally cleaves GM2 ganglioside → GM3 + GalNAc. Without Hex A, GM2 ganglioside accumulates in neuronal lysosomes → progressive neuronal destruction. Features: (1) Motor and mental regression after normal development, (2) Cherry-red spot (ganglion cell accumulation makes the macula opaque except at the fovea where there are no ganglion cells — appears red), (3) Hyperacusis (exaggerated startle to sound), (4) Macrocephaly (neuronal swelling). No organomegaly (unlike Gaucher/Niemann-Pick). Death by age 2–4. Incorrect options: (A) Glucocerebroside accumulates in GAUCHER disease (beta-glucocerebrosidase deficiency) — presents with organomegaly, bone pain, NO cherry-red spot (primarily non-neuronopathic). (C) Galactocerebroside accumulates in KRABBE disease (galactocerebrosidase deficiency) — severe early infantile onset, globoid cells. (D) Sphingomyelin accumulates in NIEMANN-PICK disease (sphingomyelinase deficiency) — foamy macrophages, cherry-red spot in type A. Exam pearl: Tay-Sachs vs Niemann-Pick: BOTH have cherry-red spot. Distinguish: Tay-Sachs = hexosaminidase A, no organomegaly; Niemann-Pick = sphingomyelinase, WITH organomegaly (splenomegaly).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old child presents with joint pain, dark-colored urine (on standing), and bluish-black discoloration of earlobes and sclera (ochronosis). Urine tests positive for reducing substances. Which metabolic pathway is disrupted?

options.A: Phenylalanine → tyrosine (phenylalanine hydroxylase deficient)
options.B: Tyrosine → fumarate + acetoacetate: homogentisate oxidase (homogentisic acid dioxygenase) deficient → accumulation of homogentisic acid (alkaptonuria)
options.C: Tryptophan → serotonin → melatonin
options.D: Methionine → homocysteine → cystathionine (cystathionine beta-synthase deficient)

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Alkaptonuria (Garrod's 'inborn error') is caused by deficiency of homogentisate oxidase (homogentisic acid dioxygenase), which is required in the tyrosine catabolism pathway. Tyrosine → 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate → homogentisate → BLOCKED → homogentisic acid accumulates. Oxidation of homogentisic acid on standing → black pigment (alkapton) → dark urine on exposure to air. Ochronosis = deposition of homogentisate polymer in connective tissue (cartilage, tendons, sclera) → bluish-black discoloration. Reduces Benedict's reagent (reducing substance). Arthropathy in older patients. Benign course; no intellectual disability. Incorrect options: (A) Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency = PKU — elevated phenylalanine, not homogentisate; no ochronosis or darkening urine. (C) Tryptophan pathway → serotonin/melatonin synthesis; disruptions cause carcinoid (↑ serotonin) or Hartnup disease (tryptophan transport) — not ochronosis. (D) CBS deficiency = homocystinuria — marfanoid habitus, lens subluxation (downward — Marfan = upward), thromboembolism — no dark urine or ochronosis. Exam pearl: Alkaptonuria = Garrod's original inborn error of metabolism. Urine darkens on standing or alkalinization. Ochronosis + arthritis in adults.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old medical student is asked about buffering. The major intracellular buffer is a combination of a weak acid and its conjugate base. Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, when the pH of a buffer equals its pKa, what is the ratio of the proton acceptor (A-) to the proton donor (HA)?
questions.explanation: Correct (C): Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). When pH = pKa: pKa = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) → log([A-]/[HA]) = 0 → [A-]/[HA] = 10^0 = 1 → ratio is 1:1. At pH = pKa, the buffer has equimolar amounts of acid and conjugate base. This is the point of MAXIMUM BUFFERING CAPACITY. Incorrect options: (A) [A-]/[HA] = 10 when pH = pKa + 1. (B) [A-]/[HA] = 0.1 when pH = pKa − 1. (D) Ratio 1:10 = [A-]/[HA] = 0.1, same as when pH is 1 unit BELOW pKa. Exam pearl: Bicarbonate buffer system: pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3-]/[H2CO3]). At normal plasma pH 7.4: log ratio = 1.3 → ratio ~20:1 (bicarbonate:carbonic acid). Bicarbonate buffer works best at pH 7.4 even though pKa is 6.1 because CO2 is continuously regulated by lungs (open system).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman with autoimmune gastritis presents with macrocytic megaloblastic anemia, glossitis, and tingling in both feet. She also has subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (loss of proprioception and vibration in lower limbs). Her serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are both elevated. Which vitamin deficiency is this and what are its TWO essential enzymatic roles?

options.A: Folate — required for dTMP synthesis and purine synthesis
options.B: Vitamin B12 — cofactor for (1) methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (converts methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA) and (2) methionine synthase (converts homocysteine → methionine, requires 5-methyl-THF)
options.C: Vitamin B6 — cofactor for aminotransferases and ALA synthase
options.D: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) — component of FAD/FMN in ETC

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency in autoimmune gastritis is due to anti-intrinsic factor antibodies → pernicious anemia. B12 serves as cofactor for TWO CRITICAL ENZYMES: (1) Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (adenosylcobalamin cofactor) — converts methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (odd-chain fatty acid and branched-chain AA catabolism). Deficiency → ↑methylmalonic acid. (2) Methionine synthase (methylcobalamin cofactor) — homocysteine + 5-methyl-THF → methionine + THF. Deficiency → ↑homocysteine, 'folate trap' (THF not regenerated → folate deficiency picture despite adequate folate). Neurological damage: myelin synthesis impaired (SAM from methionine needed for methylation reactions). Incorrect options: (A) Folate: only homocysteine elevated (not methylmalonate). Folate deficiency does NOT cause neurological symptoms. (C) B6: neuropathy + sideroblastic anemia; no methylmalonic acid or homocysteine elevation characteristically. (D) Riboflavin (B2): FAD/FMN cofactor; deficiency causes 'glossitis, cheilosis, corneal vascularization' — not megaloblastic anemia or elevated methylmalonates. Exam pearl: Schilling test: differentiates dietary B12 deficiency (corrected by oral B12) from pernicious anemia (corrected by adding intrinsic factor) from malabsorption. Elevated MMA + homocysteine = B12. Elevated homocysteine only = folate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A researcher treats isolated mitochondria with 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a proton uncoupler. She measures oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis rates. What would be the expected result?

options.A: Oxygen consumption decreases, ATP synthesis decreases
options.B: Oxygen consumption increases, ATP synthesis decreases, heat production increases
options.C: Oxygen consumption decreases, ATP synthesis increases
options.D: Both oxygen consumption and ATP synthesis increase proportionally

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Uncouplers (protonophores) like 2,4-DNP, thermogenin (UCP1 in brown fat), and oligomycin-resistant uncouplers dissipate the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane by carrying H+ ions directly across (bypassing ATP synthase). Effect: (1) Proton gradient is dissipated as HEAT (not used for ATP synthesis) → ↓ ATP synthesis. (2) Without the proton backpressure, the ETC can run FASTER (protons are not backing up) → ↑ O2 consumption (substrate oxidation continues uncoupled from ATP production). (3) Heat generation increases (thermogenesis). DNP was used as a weight loss drug in the 1930s but caused hyperthermia and death. Incorrect options: (A) O2 consumption would INCREASE, not decrease — ETC runs freely without impedance. (C) O2 increases but ATP decreases (proton gradient used for heat, not ATP). (D) If both increase proportionally, that would describe normal coupled respiration — uncouplers break this coupling. Exam pearl: Brown adipose tissue uses UCP1 (thermogenin) as a physiological uncoupler for non-shivering thermogenesis in neonates and cold adaptation. Thyroid hormone increases UCP1 expression. ATP synthase (Complex V) requires proton gradient (chemiosmosis) — Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man is diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Genetic analysis shows a point mutation in the KRAS gene (G12V). Which of the following best describes why this mutation drives cancer?

options.A: KRAS G12V gains intrinsic GTPase activity, permanently activating downstream signaling
options.B: KRAS G12V loses GTPase activity, locking KRAS in the GTP-bound (active) state, constitutively activating MAPK and PI3K pathways
options.C: KRAS G12V blocks RAS-GDP interaction, preventing signal transmission
options.D: KRAS G12V activates p53-mediated apoptosis

questions.explanation: Correct (B): RAS proteins (HRAS, KRAS, NRAS) are small GTPases. Normally: Growth factor → RTK activation → Grb2/SOS → RAS-GDP → RAS-GTP (active) → MAPK/PI3K activation → cell proliferation. RAS is inactivated by its INTRINSIC GTPase activity (GDP-bound = inactive) + GAPs (GTPase-activating proteins) accelerate GTP hydrolysis. KRAS G12V mutation (glycine → valine at codon 12) IMPAIRS the GTPase activity → GTP cannot be hydrolyzed → RAS locked in GTP-bound (active) state → CONSTITUTIVE signaling → uncontrolled proliferation. This is the most common oncogenic mutation in human cancers (KRAS, NRAS, HRAS). Incorrect options: (A) Gaining GTPase activity would INACTIVATE the signal — opposite of what causes cancer. (C) Blocking RAS-GDP would impair normal inactivation, but the mechanism of G12V is specifically impaired GTPase activity — the GTP cannot be hydrolyzed. (D) KRAS G12V SUPPRESSES apoptosis (promotes survival through Akt/BCL2 pathways) — does not activate p53-mediated apoptosis. Exam pearl: KRAS mutations in: colorectal (40%), pancreatic (90%), lung adenocarcinoma (30%). KRAS-mutated tumors are RESISTANT to EGFR inhibitors (cetuximab, panitumumab) — must test for KRAS before giving these drugs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 5-year-old child with recurrent sinopulmonary infections is found to have absent serum immunoglobulins. B cells are absent from peripheral blood. This condition (Bruton's agammaglobulinemia) is caused by a mutation in BTK (Bruton's tyrosine kinase). Where does BTK act in B cell development?

options.A: Prevents somatic hypermutation in germinal centers
options.B: Required for signaling from the pre-B cell receptor (pre-BCR) for maturation of pro-B → pre-B → immature B cells
options.C: Required for class switch recombination from IgM to IgG
options.D: Required for positive selection of B cells in the thymus

questions.explanation: Correct (B): BTK (Bruton's tyrosine kinase) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase essential for PRE-B CELL RECEPTOR (pre-BCR) signaling. In normal B cell development: stem cell → pro-B cell (VDJ recombination of heavy chain) → pre-B cell (pre-BCR = mu heavy chain + surrogate light chains) → BTK signals survival and proliferation → immature B cell → mature B cell. In BTK deficiency (X-linked agammaglobulinemia, XLA): development is arrested at the pro-B → pre-B transition in the bone marrow → no mature B cells → no immunoglobulins → recurrent bacterial infections beginning after maternal antibody wanes (~6 months). Incorrect options: (A) Somatic hypermutation occurs in germinal centers of secondary lymphoid organs after antigen encounter — BTK does act in BCR signaling but the primary developmental block is early in bone marrow. (C) Class switch recombination (IgM→IgG/IgA/IgE) requires AID (activation-induced cytidine deaminase) and occurs in germinal centers — this requires BTK for BCR signaling but the primary defect is earlier. (D) B cells develop in the BONE MARROW, not the thymus (thymus = T cell education). Exam pearl: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib) treat CLL, mantle cell lymphoma. XLA: absent B cells, absent all Ig, recurrent bacterial infections after 6 months of age, normal T cell count.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man is prescribed a cholesterol-lowering drug that works by binding bile acids in the intestinal lumen, preventing their reabsorption. Which of the following correctly explains how this leads to reduced plasma LDL?

options.A: Bile acid sequestrants directly inhibit HMG-CoA reductase in the liver
options.B: By binding bile acids in the gut, sequestrants increase fecal bile acid loss → liver upregulates cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase → ↑ cholesterol → bile acid conversion → ↓ hepatic cholesterol → SREBP activation → ↑ LDLR expression → ↓ plasma LDL
options.C: By reducing dietary fat absorption, sequestrants reduce chylomicron formation and LDL precursors
options.D: Bile acid sequestrants inhibit intestinal cholesterol absorption via NPC1L1

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colesevelam, colestipol) are anion exchange resins that bind bile acids in the intestinal lumen → prevent enterohepatic recirculation. Mechanism of LDL lowering: (1) Less bile acid recycled to liver → hepatic bile acid pool depleted → liver upregulates cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1, rate-limiting step of bile acid synthesis) to make more bile acids from cholesterol. (2) Hepatic cholesterol consumption increases → SREBP-2 activated → (a) HMG-CoA reductase upregulated (↑ cholesterol synthesis to compensate), (b) LDLR (LDL receptor) upregulated → ↑ uptake of plasma LDL → ↓ serum LDL. Incorrect options: (A) Statins directly inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, not bile acid sequestrants. (C) Bile acid sequestrants bind bile acids not dietary fat. Fat absorption is reduced somewhat but LDL reduction is via the LDLR upregulation mechanism. (D) NPC1L1 inhibition is the mechanism of EZETIMIBE — different drug class (cholesterol absorption inhibitor). Exam pearl: Bile acid sequestrants = triglyceride-RAISING (increase VLDL) — caution in hypertriglyceridemia. Side effects: constipation, bloating, impaired absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and other drugs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man presents with multiple basal cell carcinomas, severe photosensitivity, and corneal opacification after minimal sun exposure. Skin biopsy shows accumulation of thymine dimers. He is unable to perform nucleotide excision repair. What is the diagnosis and which DNA lesion is specifically repaired by nucleotide excision repair?

options.A: Fanconi anemia — interstrand cross-links
options.B: Xeroderma pigmentosum — pyrimidine dimers (thymine dimers) caused by UV radiation
options.C: Ataxia-telangiectasia — double-strand breaks
options.D: HNPCC (Lynch syndrome) — mismatch errors during DNA replication

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive defect in NUCLEOTIDE EXCISION REPAIR (NER). UV radiation causes formation of cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (thymine-thymine dimers most commonly) and 6-4 photoproducts between adjacent pyrimidines. NER corrects these bulky helix-distorting lesions by: (1) Recognition of lesion (XPC in global genome NER), (2) Local unwinding (TFIIH with XPB/XPD helicases), (3) Dual incision ~25 bp around the lesion, (4) Excision, (5) Resynthesis (Pol delta/epsilon), (6) Ligation. Without NER, UV-induced dimers accumulate → mutations in oncogenes/tumor suppressors → multiple skin cancers. Incorrect options: (A) Fanconi anemia: defective cross-link repair; presents with aplastic anemia, pancytopenia, skeletal anomalies — NOT sun sensitivity. (C) Ataxia-telangiectasia: ATM kinase deficiency → impaired double-strand break repair (NHEJ); presents with cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, immunodeficiency, radiation sensitivity. (D) HNPCC/Lynch syndrome: defective MISMATCH REPAIR (MMR) → microsatellite instability; colon/endometrial cancers — no photosensitivity. Exam pearl: DNA repair pathways: (1) BER = single base changes, (2) NER = bulky helix-distorting lesions (UV dimers), (3) MMR = replication errors, (4) NHEJ/HR = double-strand breaks. XP = NER defect.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A type 2 diabetic patient's cells show decreased GLUT4 translocation to the cell membrane in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle despite high circulating insulin. Which intracellular signaling pathway, when defective, best explains insulin resistance?

options.A: cAMP → PKA → phosphorylation of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3)
options.B: Insulin receptor → IRS-1 → PI3K → PIP3 → PDK1 → Akt (PKB) → GLUT4 vesicle translocation
options.C: Insulin receptor → Ras → MAPK → ERK2 → GLUT4 expression
options.D: GLUT1 receptor → JAK2 → STAT5 → GLUT4 transcription

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Insulin signaling for GLUT4 translocation: Insulin binds IR (insulin receptor, a tyrosine kinase) → autophosphorylation of IR → phosphorylation of IRS-1 (insulin receptor substrate-1) → PI3K recruitment → PIP2 → PIP3 (by PI3K) → PDK1 activation → Akt (PKB) phosphorylation → AS160 phosphorylation → Rab GTPase activation → GLUT4-containing vesicle fusion with plasma membrane. In T2DM (insulin resistance): defects in IRS-1, PI3K, or Akt activity → impaired GLUT4 translocation → glucose not taken up despite high insulin. Incorrect options: (A) cAMP/PKA pathway is activated by GLUCAGON and epinephrine — promotes glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and lipolysis — OPPOSITE of insulin action. (C) Ras/MAPK pathway is activated by insulin but drives CELL GROWTH/MITOGENESIS, not primarily GLUT4 translocation. (D) GLUT1 is not a receptor; JAK-STAT is used by cytokines and growth hormone, not insulin (primarily). Exam pearl: Two main insulin signaling arms: PI3K/Akt → metabolic effects (glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis, anti-lipolysis). MAPK/ERK → mitogenic effects (cell growth, protein synthesis). Insulin resistance mainly affects PI3K/Akt arm, not MAPK arm.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A premature neonate at 28 weeks is born in respiratory distress. Chest X-ray shows bilateral ground-glass opacification. Which biochemical deficiency is responsible and what is the biochemical structure of the deficient substance?

options.A: Deficiency of surfactant protein B only — protein component not lipid
options.B: Deficiency of pulmonary surfactant (primarily dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine/DPPC, a saturated phospholipid) synthesized by type II pneumocytes
options.C: Deficiency of mucus glycoproteins lining bronchioles
options.D: Deficiency of immunoglobulin A in bronchial secretions

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) / hyaline membrane disease is due to surfactant deficiency in premature infants (<35 weeks). Pulmonary surfactant: (1) Lipid composition: ~80% phospholipids — predominantly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC, lecithin) — both fatty acid chains are SATURATED palmitate (C16:0). Also contains phosphatidylglycerol (PG). (2) Protein components: SP-A, SP-B, SP-C, SP-D (surfactant proteins). DPPC reduces alveolar surface tension at low lung volumes, preventing alveolar collapse (atelectasis). L:S ratio (lecithin:sphingomyelin) <2 in amniotic fluid indicates surfactant immaturity. Treatment: antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) to induce surfactant production + exogenous surfactant after birth. Incorrect options: (A) Surfactant is primarily a LIPID (DPPC), not just protein. SP-B deficiency alone causes a specific form but the main deficiency in prematurity is overall surfactant. (C) Mucus glycoproteins are deficient in cystic fibrosis (abnormal CFTR → thick mucus) — not RDS. (D) IgA deficiency causes recurrent infections — not respiratory distress in a neonate. Exam pearl: L:S ratio >2 = lung maturity. Betamethasone/dexamethasone crosses placenta → induces type II pneumocyte maturation → surfactant synthesis. Surfactant = 'DPPC + PG + SP-A/B/C/D'.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman taking methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis develops megaloblastic anemia and mucositis. Methotrexate inhibits DHFR. Which metabolic consequence directly causes the megaloblastic changes?

options.A: Impaired synthesis of deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP), causing accumulation of uracil in DNA
options.B: Impaired synthesis of deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) from dUMP due to lack of 5,10-methylene-THF → 'thymidine starvation' → impaired DNA synthesis
options.C: Impaired methylation of homocysteine → elevated homocysteine
options.D: Impaired synthesis of glutamine, a key purine precursor

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Methotrexate (MTX) inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) → cannot regenerate THF from DHF → THF pool depleted → insufficient 5,10-methylene-THF → thymidylate synthase (TS) cannot convert dUMP → dTMP (thymidylate). Result: THYMIDYLATE STARVATION → dTTP depleted → DNA synthesis impaired → cells trying to replicate use dUTP → uracil misincorporated into DNA (excised → DNA breaks) → rapidly dividing cells (GI mucosa, bone marrow) affected → megaloblastic anemia + mucositis. This is 'thymineless death.' Leucovorin (5-formyl-THF, folinic acid) rescues by bypassing DHFR. Incorrect options: (A) dUMP accumulates (it is not converted to dTMP) but it is the LACK of dTMP (thymidine starvation) that causes the megaloblastic changes. dUMP buildup and uracil misincorporation are consequences but the primary issue is dTMP deficiency. (C) Impaired homocysteine methylation occurs when methionine synthase is impaired (B12 deficiency via folate trap) but this is not the PRIMARY cause of megaloblastic changes with MTX. (D) MTX does impair purine synthesis (10-formyl-THF needed) — contributes to megaloblastic anemia — but the most DIRECT and classic teaching answer is dTMP deficiency. Exam pearl: MTX mechanism: DHFR inhibition → no THF → no 5,10-methylene-THF → TS blocked → no dTMP = thymidylate synthesis blocked. Leucovorin rescue bypasses DHFR.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man is admitted with a myocardial infarction. His CRP (C-reactive protein) is markedly elevated. Which of the following correctly describes CRP?

options.A: CRP is a negative acute phase protein synthesized in the spleen, decreasing during inflammation
options.B: CRP is a positive acute phase protein synthesized by hepatocytes, stimulated by IL-6; it opsonizes bacteria and activates complement
options.C: CRP is an immunoglobulin synthesized by plasma cells during immune response
options.D: CRP is an enzyme secreted by neutrophils to destroy bacterial cell walls

questions.explanation: Correct (B): CRP (C-reactive protein) is the prototypical positive acute phase reactant: (1) Synthesized by HEPATOCYTES (not immune cells). (2) Stimulated by cytokines IL-6 (primary), IL-1, TNF-alpha released during inflammation. (3) Rises within 6 hours of tissue injury, peaks at 48–72 hours, half-life ~19 hours. (4) FUNCTIONS: Binds phosphocholine on bacterial surfaces and apoptotic cells → activates complement (classical pathway, C1q) → opsonization → phagocytosis. CRP levels used to assess cardiovascular risk and monitor inflammatory disease activity. Incorrect options: (A) NEGATIVE acute phase proteins (decrease during acute phase): albumin, transferrin, prealbumin (transthyretin), retinol-binding protein — these decrease because the liver diverts resources to making positive APPs. (C) CRP is a pentraxin (5-ringed protein), not an immunoglobulin. It does NOT have antigen-specific binding. (D) CRP is NOT an enzyme and is not secreted by neutrophils. Lysozyme is a neutrophil enzyme that destroys bacterial peptidoglycan. Exam pearl: Positive APPs: CRP, fibrinogen, SAA (serum amyloid A), haptoglobin, ferritin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, complement. SAA → amyloid A → AA amyloidosis in chronic inflammation. ESR: elevated in inflammation, anemia, pregnancy; decreased in polycythemia, sickle cell.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A researcher studies oxidative stress in a cell culture. Which enzyme is the FIRST LINE of defense against superoxide radicals (O2•-) generated in mitochondria?

options.A: Catalase
options.B: Glutathione peroxidase
options.C: Superoxide dismutase (SOD)
options.D: NADPH oxidase

questions.explanation: Correct (C): Superoxide dismutase (SOD) catalyzes: 2O2•- + 2H+ → H2O2 + O2. This is the FIRST line of defense against superoxide. Isoforms: MnSOD (SOD2, mitochondria), Cu/ZnSOD (SOD1, cytoplasm), and extracellular CuZnSOD (SOD3). After SOD converts O2•- to H2O2: (1) Catalase (peroxisomes): 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2. (2) Glutathione peroxidase (cytosol/mitochondria, selenium-dependent): H2O2 + 2GSH → GSSG + 2H2O. Incorrect options: (A) Catalase decomposes H2O2 (NOT superoxide directly) — acts AFTER SOD. (B) Glutathione peroxidase decomposes H2O2 and lipid peroxides — acts AFTER SOD. (D) NADPH oxidase generates superoxide (O2•-) in phagocytes (respiratory burst) — it is a SOURCE, not a defense. Deficiency = Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD). Exam pearl: Sequence: Superoxide (O2•-) → SOD → H2O2 → Catalase/GPx → H2O. Fenton reaction: H2O2 + Fe2+ → OH• (hydroxyl radical — most reactive ROS). Paraquat poisoning → generates superoxide → overwhelming oxidative stress.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A mutation in a splice site sequence of a gene causes an exon to be retained in the mature mRNA, disrupting the reading frame and causing a premature stop codon. Which of the following correctly describes NORMAL pre-mRNA splicing and the splicing machinery?

options.A: Splicing is carried out by ribosomes in the cytoplasm, removing introns from fully exported mRNA
options.B: Splicing is carried out in the nucleus by the spliceosome — a large ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex containing snRNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) that recognizes consensus splice site sequences (5'-GU...AG-3' rule) and performs two transesterification reactions
options.C: Splicing removes exons and joins introns to form the mature coding RNA
options.D: Splicing is performed by group I and II self-splicing ribozymes in all eukaryotic genes

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Pre-mRNA splicing removes introns and joins exons. The spliceosome: (1) Composed of 5 snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs): U1, U2, U4, U5, U6 + associated proteins (snRNPs). (2) U1 snRNP recognizes the 5' splice site (GU at intron start). U2 snRNP binds the branch point (adenosine residue ~15–50 nt upstream of 3' splice site). U4/U5/U6 complete assembly. (3) Two transesterification reactions: lariat formation + exon ligation. Splice sites: ALWAYS 5'-GU...AG-3' ('GT-AG rule'). Mutations here cause aberrant splicing. Incorrect options: (A) Splicing occurs in the NUCLEUS before mRNA export. Ribosomes translate mRNA in the cytoplasm AFTER splicing. (C) Exactly reversed — splicing removes INTRONS (non-coding), joins EXONS (coding sequences). (D) Self-splicing group I and II ribozymes exist in some organisms/organelles (e.g., Tetrahymena rRNA, mitochondrial introns) but the vast majority of nuclear eukaryotic pre-mRNA requires the SPLICEOSOME. Exam pearl: Alternative splicing allows one gene to produce multiple protein isoforms. Aberrant splicing causes numerous genetic diseases (e.g., β-thalassemia, Gaucher disease splice-site mutations).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman is found to have low serum albumin (2.0 g/dL), pitting edema, and normal liver function. She is on a very low-protein diet. On electrophoresis, albumin band is markedly reduced. Which of the following is the PRIMARY function of albumin that explains the edema?

options.A: Albumin transports oxygen from lungs to tissues
options.B: Albumin maintains plasma oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure, preventing fluid leakage into the interstitium
options.C: Albumin binds and transports ionized calcium in blood
options.D: Albumin is the primary buffer of the blood

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Albumin (MW ~66 kDa) is the most abundant plasma protein (3.5–5 g/dL) and is the principal determinant of plasma oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure (~80% of oncotic pressure). At the capillary level, oncotic pressure opposes hydrostatic pressure (Starling forces). When albumin falls (malnutrition, nephrotic syndrome, liver failure): ↓ oncotic pressure → fluid leaves capillaries into interstitium → edema. Incorrect options: (A) Oxygen is transported by HEMOGLOBIN in RBCs — not albumin. (C) Ionized calcium is the active physiological form. TOTAL serum calcium = ionized (50%) + protein-bound (40%, mainly albumin) + complexed (10%). Low albumin → low TOTAL calcium but ionized Ca2+ is NORMAL (relevant correction: corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.8 × (4.0 - albumin)). Albumin does bind calcium but this is not its primary function. (D) The bicarbonate buffer system (primarily) and hemoglobin, phosphate, and proteins collectively buffer blood. While albumin does have buffering capacity (histidine residues), this is not its PRIMARY function. Exam pearl: Oncotic pressure: 25–28 mmHg contributed mainly by albumin. Low albumin causes edema (nephrotic syndrome, kwashiorkor, cirrhosis). Kwashiorkor = protein deficiency; Marasmus = total calorie deficiency (no edema in marasmus).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A biochemist is studying the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). Which of the following correctly describes ALL the major products of the OXIDATIVE phase of the PPP from glucose-6-phosphate?

options.A: 2 NADH + ATP + pyruvate
options.B: 2 NADPH + CO2 + ribulose-5-phosphate
options.C: 1 FADH2 + 1 NADPH + oxaloacetate
options.D: 2 ATP + 2 NADPH + fructose-6-phosphate

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The OXIDATIVE phase of the PPP: (Step 1) Glucose-6-phosphate + NADP+ → 6-phosphogluconolactone + NADPH + H+ [G6PD — rate-limiting]. (Step 2) 6-phosphogluconolactone → 6-phosphogluconate [lactonase]. (Step 3) 6-phosphogluconate + NADP+ → Ribulose-5-phosphate + CO2 + NADPH + H+ [6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase]. NET: glucose-6-phosphate + 2NADP+ → ribulose-5-phosphate + CO2 + 2NADPH. The products are: 2 NADPH (reducing power for glutathione reduction, fatty acid synthesis, etc.), 1 CO2, and ribulose-5-phosphate (pentose for nucleotide synthesis). Incorrect options: (A) 2 NADH + ATP + pyruvate = glycolysis products — not PPP. (C) FADH2/OAA = TCA cycle intermediates. (D) ATP is NOT produced in PPP; fructose-6-phosphate is a product of the NON-OXIDATIVE phase (transketolase/transaldolase reactions). Exam pearl: PPP purposes: (1) NADPH production (reductive biosynthesis, antioxidant defense via glutathione), (2) Ribose-5-phosphate (nucleotide synthesis). RBCs rely entirely on PPP for NADPH. PPP is most active in: liver, lactating mammary gland, adrenal cortex (steroidogenesis), RBCs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old boy from a rural area has low height, delayed puberty, hypogonadism, hepatosplenomegaly, and a history of eating clay (pica). Serum mineral levels show a specific trace element deficiency. What is the most likely deficiency and its role in the body?

options.A: Selenium deficiency — component of glutathione peroxidase (antioxidant defense)
options.B: Zinc deficiency — cofactor for >300 enzymes; required for gonadal development (testosterone production), immune function (thymulin), and wound healing
options.C: Copper deficiency — needed for lysyl oxidase (collagen cross-linking) and ceruloplasmin
options.D: Manganese deficiency — cofactor for mitochondrial SOD (MnSOD)

questions.explanation: Correct (B): The clinical picture — growth retardation, delayed puberty/hypogonadism, pica (eating clay/geophagus, which impairs zinc absorption), hepatosplenomegaly — is classic for ZINC deficiency (originally described by Ananda Prasad in Iran/Egypt). Zinc is: (1) Cofactor for >300 metalloenzymes (carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, alcohol dehydrogenase, matrix metalloproteinases). (2) Essential for gonadal development and testosterone synthesis. (3) Required for thymulin activity → immune function, T-cell maturation. (4) Needed for wound healing, taste perception (gustin), and vision (retinol dehydrogenase). (5) Component of zinc finger motifs in transcription factors. Clay eating depletes zinc by competitive absorption inhibition. Incorrect options: (A) Selenium deficiency: Keshan disease (cardiomyopathy in China), Kashin-Beck disease (arthropathy), thyroid dysfunction — not the described syndrome. (C) Copper deficiency: Menkes disease (X-linked) in children — kinky hair, mental retardation, low serum copper/ceruloplasmin, defective cross-linking — no hypogonadism. (D) Manganese deficiency is rare in humans; excessive manganese causes 'manganism' (parkinsonian features). Exam pearl: Zinc deficiency: growth retardation + hypogonadism + pica + dermatitis + dysgeusia. Acrodermatitis enteropathica = autosomal recessive zinc malabsorption.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy presents with marfanoid habitus, downward lens subluxation, intellectual disability, and a DVT. Urine shows a positive nitroprusside test. Which enzyme is deficient and which vitamins may help if the enzyme has residual activity?

options.A: Homocystinuria due to CBS deficiency (B6, B12, folate may reduce homocysteine); or methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency (treated with folate/betaine)
options.B: Cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS) deficiency → homocystinuria. If residual enzyme activity (B6-responsive form), pyridoxine reduces homocysteine; also betaine (alternative remethylation)
options.C: Methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency → SAM deficiency only
options.D: Cystathionase deficiency → cystathioninuria

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Homocystinuria (classic): Autosomal recessive deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS). CBS converts homocysteine + serine → cystathionine (requires PLP/B6 as cofactor). Deficiency → homocysteine accumulates → cysteine becomes essential. Clinical features: MARFANOID habitus (tall, arachnodactyly — but NOT like Marfan; CBS = downward lens subluxation vs Marfan = upward), intellectual disability, psychiatric issues, thromboembolic events (DVT, stroke — due to endothelial damage by homocysteine). Nitroprusside test positive for homocysteine in urine. Treatment: (1) B6 (pyridoxine) — reduces homocysteine if enzyme has residual activity (B6-responsive in ~50%); (2) Low methionine diet; (3) Betaine (provides alternative methyl group for homocysteine remethylation to methionine); (4) Folate + B12 (support methionine synthase pathway). Incorrect options: (A) Partially correct — but the most direct and complete answer is B. MTHFR deficiency is a separate condition (mild hyperhomocysteinemia, thrombosis without full marfanoid habitus). (C) MAT deficiency causes isolated hypermethioninemia without marked homocystinuria. (D) Cystathionase deficiency: cystathioninuria — BENIGN, no clinical disease. Exam pearl: Homocystinuria = downward lens dislocation + DVT/stroke + marfanoid + intellectual disability. Marfan = upward lens. Both autosomal. In Marfan, no homocysteine elevation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A patient taking aspirin for secondary prevention of MI wants to understand its mechanism. Which enzyme does aspirin irreversibly inhibit, and what is the consequence in platelets specifically?

options.A: Aspirin inhibits phospholipase A2 → prevents arachidonic acid release from membrane phospholipids
options.B: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) → prevents thromboxane A2 (TXA2) synthesis in platelets → inhibits platelet aggregation for platelet's lifetime (~7–10 days) since platelets cannot synthesize new COX
options.C: Aspirin inhibits lipoxygenase → prevents leukotriene synthesis → anti-inflammatory
options.D: Aspirin inhibits prostacyclin synthase in endothelium → prevents PGI2 formation → anti-aggregatory

questions.explanation: Correct (B): Aspirin mechanism: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) covalently ACETYLATES a serine residue (Ser-530 in COX-1, Ser-516 in COX-2) in the active site of COX enzymes → IRREVERSIBLE inhibition. In PLATELETS: COX-1 is constitutively expressed → makes TXA2 (from arachidonic acid via PGH2). TXA2 promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. Platelets are ANUCLEATE → cannot synthesize new COX → blocked for their entire lifespan (7–10 days). Low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg) selectively inhibits platelet COX-1 (portal effect — inactivates platelets in portal circulation before systemic absorption). ENDOTHELIAL CELLS can synthesize new COX → continue to make PGI2 (prostacyclin) — anti-aggregatory and vasodilatory. Incorrect options: (A) Corticosteroids inhibit phospholipase A2 (via annexin/lipocortin induction) — not aspirin. Aspirin acts DOWNSTREAM of arachidonic acid release. (C) NSAIDs do NOT inhibit lipoxygenase (5-LOX) — that pathway makes leukotrienes, inhibited by zileuton. (D) Aspirin inhibits prostacyclin synthase is incorrect; it inhibits COX, which reduces PGH2 (substrate for both TXA2 in platelets and PGI2 in endothelium) — but the NET effect on platelets > endothelium gives anti-aggregatory outcome. Exam pearl: COX-1 = constitutive (platelets, GI protection). COX-2 = inducible (inflammation). Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) → anti-inflammatory without GI side effects but ↑ cardiovascular risk (less prostacyclin protection). Aspirin overdose = Reye's syndrome in children (never give aspirin to children with viral illness).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question_text: A 6-month-old infant presents with severe lactic acidosis, psychomotor delay, and episodic neurological crises worsened by carbohydrate feeding. MRI shows bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem lesions (Leigh syndrome). Enzyme studies confirm pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) deficiency. Which is the DIRECT biochemical consequence?

options.A: Pyruvate cannot be carboxylated to oxaloacetate → gluconeogenesis impaired
options.B: Pyruvate cannot be decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA → accumulates as pyruvate/lactate + alanine; TCA cycle and OXPHOS starved of acetyl-CoA; brain (highly aerobic) most affected
options.C: Pyruvate cannot be reduced to lactate → increased glycolysis
options.D: Acetyl-CoA cannot enter the TCA cycle → increased ketone body synthesis

questions.explanation: Correct (B): PDC (pyruvate dehydrogenase complex) catalyzes the IRREVERSIBLE oxidative decarboxylation: Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA → Acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH. PDC is the bridge between glycolysis and the TCA cycle. PDC deficiency: (1) Pyruvate accumulates → shunted to LACTATE (by LDH) → lactic acidosis; and ALANINE (by alanine aminotransferase). (2) No acetyl-CoA produced from carbohydrates → TCA cycle and OXPHOS are substrate-deprived → ATP deficiency → brain (most energy-dependent, aerobic organ) suffers most → Leigh syndrome (subacute necrotizing encephalopathy). (3) Worsened by CARBOHYDRATE feeding (more pyruvate → more lactic acid). (4) Improved by ketogenic diet (provides acetyl-CoA via fatty acid oxidation, bypassing PDC). PDC requires 5 cofactors: TPP (B1), lipoate, CoA (B5), FAD (B2), NAD+ (B3). Incorrect options: (A) Carboxylation of pyruvate to OAA is the role of PYRUVATE CARBOXYLASE (separate enzyme, biotin-dependent) — different deficiency. (C) Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) reduces pyruvate → lactate — this is INTACT in PDC deficiency (it is the compensation). (D) Fatty acid oxidation produces acetyl-CoA independent of PDC — ketone bodies are not deficient; in fact, ketogenic diet TREATS PDC deficiency. Exam pearl: PDC cofactors (B vitamins): TPP (B1), Lipoic acid, CoA (pantothenate, B5), FAD (B2), NAD (B3). Leigh syndrome: most common cause = Complex I deficiency or PDC deficiency; maternal inheritance if mtDNA mutation.
